ut_copperhead_boulder.blurb: A single boulder, sitting among the first cluster of blocks beside the trail up from the parking lot at the foot of Little Cottonwood Canyon. It holds about two dozen problems on quartz monzonite, spread widely: a handful of easy lines near V0 to V2, a few mid-grade problems around V4, and then a long run of hard ones from the V6 range up past V10. The overhanging face is crimpy and tough on skin, and it hosts one of the canyon's best-known old-school test pieces. Moderate climbers find a couple of famous lines here, while strong boulderers get plenty to try. Expect company, as this is among the canyon's busiest boulder groups, and summer heat can make it unpleasant.

ut_pete_s_rock.blurb: A small quartzite outcrop on the east bench of Salt Lake City, right beside the start of the Mount Olympus hike, with a wide view over the valley. Most of the 25 climbs here are trad lines, with a few boulder problems, a couple of top-rope lines and a lone sport route. Routes mostly fall between 5.6 and 5.11, centered on the 5.8 to 5.10 range, and the boulder problems run from VB up to about V3. Short and close to town, it suits quick after-work sessions, teaching days and club outings rather than big objectives. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons since the rock is exposed and gets hot on summer afternoons.

ut_jhcob_wall.blurb: One of Big Cottonwood Canyon's better-known cliffs, rising on the south side of the road a couple of miles up from the canyon mouth, near a roadside pullout with an interpretive sign. Climbing is on quartzite and mostly traditional, with some bolted lines and a lone ice route; many lines are one to four pitches with real exposure. Grades run from easy fifth class near 5.6 up to hard 5.13 test pieces, with the bulk between 5.6 and 5.11. Its north-facing side stays in shade. Loose rock lies above the road and a helmet is wise. Also called Jacob Wall, it suits parties comfortable placing their own gear.

ut_cannabis_wall.blurb: A cool, shady limestone wall in American Fork Canyon, just down the river from the Membrane. All 25 routes are sport climbs, and they lean hard: a single easy line and a couple around 5.10, then a core of 5.11 and 5.12 and a big cluster of 5.13, with a pair of 5.14s at the top end. It is built for strong climbers on steep, pocketed rock, and it is best suited to the summer months when the canyon runs hot and this wall holds the shade. Not a beginner stop. The approach drops to the river, so plan for the crossing.

ut_cougar_cliffs.blurb: A roadside sandstone cliff a short drive north of St. George on Highway 18. The 25 climbs are mostly bolted sport routes, with one trad line, one top rope and a few boulder problems up to a hard V8. Sport grades concentrate between 5.9 and 5.11, with a couple of easier lines in the 5.7 and 5.8 range, so it favors solid intermediate climbers more than beginners. The rock is soft, gritty and sometimes loose, giving the place a somewhat adventurous feel, and it needs a long dry spell after any rain before it is safe to climb. A good option in the cooler months when the desert is too hot elsewhere.

ut_dry_wall_the.blurb: The most popular crag in Echo Canyon, east of Park City along the interstate. A tall conglomerate wall with a long, gentle overhang that keeps routes dry through most storms. All 25 climbs are bolted sport routes with pocketed, technical movement, and the grades run steeply upward: a few at 5.10, a handful of 5.11 and 5.12, and a big group at 5.13. Rock quality varies from solid to suspect, and some of the harder starts begin in a cave where a stick clip helps. The wall catches morning sun and falls into shade by afternoon. The walk from the road to the base is only a minute or two.
ut_dry_wall_the.approach: A very short walk from the road to the base of the wall.

ut_left_side_cragging.blurb: The busiest section of the shady side of Day Canyon, reached from Potash Road outside Moab. All 25 routes in this sandstone area are traditional, many of them cracks, and a few can be found as sport or top-rope too. Grades start at about 5.9 and cluster in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a single 5.13 at the top. The canyon feels remote and quiet compared with the roadside walls near the river, and the walls grow taller as you walk in. Moab sandstone is fragile when damp, so choose dry conditions. A good fit for a competent trad party looking for crack climbing out of the sun.
